explanation.common_trap: Confusing selection bias (who enters the study) with attrition bias (who leaves the study); they threaten validity differently.

stem: A child who was bitten by a dog now fears all animals, including cats. Which classical conditioning process best explains this generalization?

spontaneous recovery, in which an extinguished response returns after a rest period
higher-order conditioning, in which the conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus
stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus

wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

stem: After learning a list of new vocabulary, a student forgets words from an earlier list learned the same day. Which interference type is responsible?

stem: A radiologist improves at detecting subtle lung nodules on CT scans after training. Colleagues note the radiologist also develops more false positives. What does this change reflect in signal detection theory?

choices.text: adaptation, in which repeated exposure to lung nodules raises the detection threshold
improved sensitivity (d prime), meaning the radiologist is better at discriminating signals from noise without criterion change
a lowered response criterion (liberal bias), meaning the radiologist is more willing to report a signal, increasing both hits and false alarms
the absolute threshold has decreased, so weaker signals now reach awareness

explanation.short: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently.
explanation.detailed: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.

wrong_answer_explanations.B: Improved d prime would increase hits without proportionally increasing false alarms; the increase in false positives indicates a criterion shift, not sensitivity change

stem: A teenager argues that civil disobedience against an unjust law is morally justified based on abstract principles of justice. According to Kohlberg, which stage of moral reasoning does this represent?

choices.text: centration, the tendency to focus on only one perceptual dimension at a time
conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance
egocentrism, the inability to adopt another person's perspective
object permanence, understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight

explanation.short: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning.
explanation.detailed: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Centration is the error the 4-year-old makes (focusing only on height); the 7-year-old has overcome centration, not exhibited it
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Egocentrism is characteristic of preoperational thought; conservation is the achievement that marks concrete operations
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage (~8–12 months); the 7-year-old described is demonstrating concrete operational thought

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Conservation = concrete operational. Object permanence = sensorimotor. Egocentrism = preoperational. Abstract morality = Kohlberg postconventional.
explanation.common_trap: Placing conservation in the wrong Piaget stage; it appears at concrete operational (~7), not preoperational.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A jury member initially unsure of a defendant's guilt shifts to a confident guilty vote after group deliberation. No new evidence was presented. Which social phenomenon best explains this shift?

choices.text: social loafing, in which individual effort decreases when working collectively
groupthink, in which the desire for group consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation
group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position
deindividuation, in which anonymity in groups leads to reduced self-awareness and more impulsive behavior

explanation.short: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk).
explanation.detailed: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Social loafing involves reduced individual effort in groups; this scenario is about opinion shift, not effort reduction
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Groupthink involves suppression of dissenting views to maintain cohesion; group polarization can occur even without pressure to conform, simply through discussion
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Deindividuation involves anonymity (e.g., crowds, online) reducing individual identity; this scenario is a deliberating jury, not an anonymous setting

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Group polarization: discussion → more extreme version of initial majority lean. Groupthink: pressure to conform → poor decisions.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing group polarization (direction determined by pre-existing lean) with groupthink (pressure-based conformity).

stem: An observer sees a student fail an exam and concludes the student is lazy, not considering that the exam was unusually difficult. Which attribution error does this illustrate?

choices.text: the mere exposure effect, in which familiarity with the victim increases helping behavior
social comparison, in which individuals evaluate their prosocial behaviors against group norms
diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act
social facilitation, in which the presence of others improves an individual's performance on helping tasks

explanation.short: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies.
explanation.detailed: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The mere exposure effect increases positive feelings toward familiar stimuli; familiarity is not described in this scenario
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Social comparison involves evaluating one's own performance or opinions relative to others; diffusion of responsibility is the specific mechanism of bystander non-helping
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Social facilitation improves performance on well-learned tasks; it does not explain reduced helping in emergencies with multiple bystanders

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Bystander effect: more people → less helping. FAE: underestimate situation, overestimate disposition.
explanation.common_trap: Thinking larger groups are more likely to help; counterintuitively, more bystanders reduce individual intervention.

passage.text: Kinetic characterization of competitive inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase by a novel antifolate compound. Background: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is a validated drug target in oncology. We investigated the inhibitory mechanism of antifolate compound AF-29 on human DHFR. stem: A student under chronic exam stress shows elevated cortisol, reduced lymphocyte proliferation, and increased rates of upper respiratory infections. Which pathway best connects stress to immune suppression?

choices.text: stress increases glucagon secretion, which diverts glucose from immune cells to muscle
the sympathetic nervous system directly destroys lymphocytes through catecholamine toxicity
stress lowers insulin, reducing glucose uptake in lymphocytes and impairing antibody production
chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity

explanation.short: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production.
explanation.detailed: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Glucagon raises blood glucose but does not selectively divert glucose away from immune cells; the HPA-cortisol axis is the primary neuroimmune link
wrong_answer_explanations.B: While the SNS releases catecholamines during acute stress, lymphocyte destruction by catecholamines is not the primary mechanism; HPA-cortisol suppression is more significant in chronic stress
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Insulin affects glucose uptake broadly; the immune suppression in chronic stress is primarily mediated by cortisol's anti-inflammatory and lympholytic effects
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Chronic stress → cortisol (HPA axis) → immune suppression. GAS stages: alarm → resistance → exhaustion.
explanation.common_trap: Attributing all stress-immune effects to the sympathetic nervous system; the HPA-cortisol axis is the key chronic stress pathway.

choices.text: Weber proposed that stratification is entirely determined by means of production, as described in Marxist class theory
Weber argued that religious beliefs (Protestant ethic) are the only meaningful dimension of social stratification
Weber proposed that biological differences between groups explain most variation in social position
Weber identified class (economic), status (social prestige), and party/power (political influence) as three distinct, partially independent dimensions of stratification

explanation.short: Weber's tripartite model: (1) Class = economic position/market. (2) Status = social honor/prestige. (3) Party/Power = political influence. These can be aligned or misaligned (e.g., 'nouveau riche' has class but may lack status).

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Marx focused on means of production and class conflict; Weber agreed class matters but added status and power as separate dimensions
wrong_answer_explanations.B: While Weber analyzed the Protestant ethic and capitalism, he proposed the tripartite model of stratification as a distinct contribution, not religion alone
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Weber's stratification model is sociological, not biological; he emphasized social structures, not biological determinism
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

stem: Research consistently shows that lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher rates of cardiovascular disease, even after controlling for behaviors like smoking and diet. Which explanatory framework best accounts for this residual association?

social mobility eliminates the health gradient because individuals can improve their SES over time
lower SES individuals have genetic variants that directly cause cardiovascular disease

structural and psychosocial mechanisms including chronic stress from financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and adverse neighborhood environments that persist independently of individual behaviors

wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

violation of a social norm enforced by informal negative sanctions (social exclusion), not a formal rule or law

explanation.detailed: Norms: mores (strong moral significance), folkways (everyday courtesy, minor infractions), taboos (strongest prohibitions). explanation.common_trap: Classifying all norm violations as mores; mores carry strong moral condemnation, while folkways are everyday courtesy rules.

stem: In a randomized controlled trial, an experimental drug reduces cholesterol by 30 mg/dL (p = 0.001, 95% CI: 20–40 mg/dL). Which statement best interprets these results?

the sample size was too small to detect a true causal relationship

explanation.detailed: Observational studies establish associations, not causation. Establishing causation requires ruling out confounders, reverse causation, and chance. stem: A child who was bitten by a dog now fears all animals, including cats. Which classical conditioning process best explains this generalization?

stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus
flooding, in which maximum exposure to the feared stimulus eliminates the response
spontaneous recovery, in which an extinguished response returns after a rest period

stem: A student studies for an exam in the same room where the exam will be held, performing better than classmates who studied elsewhere. Which memory principle explains this?

choices.text: encoding specificity, in which retrieval is enhanced when the context at retrieval matches the context during encoding
the spacing effect, in which distributed practice improves recall compared to massed practice
consolidation, in which memories are transferred from short-term to long-term storage during sleep
proactive interference, in which old memories disrupt retrieval of new information

explanation.short: Encoding specificity principle (Tulving): memory is best when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions (same room, same state, same cues). Context-dependent and state-dependent memory are related phenomena.
explanation.detailed: Encoding specificity principle (Tulving): memory is best when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions (same room, same state, same cues). Context-dependent and state-dependent memory are related phenomena. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: encoding specificity, in which retrieval is enhanced when the context at retrieval matches the context during encoding.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: The spacing effect describes better memory from distributed study sessions; the benefit here is context matching, not spacing
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Consolidation explains why sleep improves memory; the effect described is about environmental context at retrieval
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Proactive interference is when old memories block new learning; this scenario describes a context-match benefit, not interference

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Encoding specificity: memory is cue-dependent. Motor skills = procedural (implicit, basal ganglia/cerebellum). Episodic memories = declarative (explicit, hippocampus).

stem: After learning a list of new vocabulary, a student forgets words from an earlier list learned the same day. Which interference type is responsible?

choices.text: the serial position effect, in which primacy and recency determine recall regardless of similar material
motivated forgetting, in which anxiety about language learning suppresses both sets of memories
proactive interference, in which older learned material (French) interferes with the encoding or retrieval of newer material (Spanish)
retroactive interference, in which newer material disrupts recall of older material

explanation.short: Proactive: PRO-old interferes with new. Retroactive: RETRO-new interferes with old (going backward). Memory tip: Pro-active = old moving Forward and blocking new; Retro-active = new going Backward and erasing old.
explanation.detailed: Proactive: PRO-old interferes with new. Retroactive: RETRO-new interferes with old (going backward). Memory tip: Pro-active = old moving Forward and blocking new; Retro-active = new going Backward and erasing old. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: proactive interference, in which older learned material (French) interferes with the encoding or retrieval of newer material (Spanish).

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The serial position effect describes recall patterns within a list based on position; it does not involve cross-list interference from similar content
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Motivated forgetting involves emotionally aversive material; learning two languages is not described as anxiety-inducing in this scenario
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts old memories; here old learning (French) disrupts new learning (Spanish), which is proactive

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Proactive: old→new disruption. Retroactive: new→old disruption.
explanation.common_trap: Reversing the direction; proactive interference comes from PRIOR learning, not new learning.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.text: Activating mutations in receptor tyrosine kinases drive concurrent MAPK and PI3K pathway activation in non-small cell lung carcinoma. the lack of a negative control means any observed effect could be due to handling alone

stem: A radiologist improves at detecting subtle lung nodules on CT scans after training. Colleagues note the radiologist also develops more false positives. What does this change reflect in signal detection theory?

choices.text: adaptation, in which repeated exposure to lung nodules raises the detection threshold
the absolute threshold has decreased, so weaker signals now reach awareness
a lowered response criterion (liberal bias), meaning the radiologist is more willing to report a signal, increasing both hits and false alarms
improved sensitivity (d prime), meaning the radiologist is better at discriminating signals from noise without criterion change

explanation.short: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently.
explanation.detailed: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: a lowered response criterion (liberal bias), meaning the radiologist is more willing to report a signal, increasing both hits and false alarms.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Adaptation reduces responsiveness to a repeated stimulus; training in detection improves, not impairs, task performance
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Absolute threshold involves the minimum detectable stimulus intensity in isolation; signal detection theory addresses detection in noise, and criterion is distinct from threshold
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Improved d prime would increase hits without proportionally increasing false alarms; the increase in false positives indicates a criterion shift, not sensitivity change

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: SDT: d' = sensitivity (independent of willingness). Criterion = willingness to report. Liberal → more hits + more false alarms.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that 'better at detecting' always means higher sensitivity (d'); it may instead reflect a shifted criterion.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A teenager argues that civil disobedience against an unjust law is morally justified based on abstract principles of justice. According to Kohlberg, which stage of moral reasoning does this represent?

choices.text: egocentrism, the inability to adopt another person's perspective
object permanence, understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight
centration, the tendency to focus on only one perceptual dimension at a time
conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance

explanation.short: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning.
explanation.detailed: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Egocentrism is characteristic of preoperational thought; conservation is the achievement that marks concrete operations
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage (~8–12 months); the 7-year-old described is demonstrating concrete operational thought
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Centration is the error the 4-year-old makes (focusing only on height); the 7-year-old has overcome centration, not exhibited it
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Conservation = concrete operational. Object permanence = sensorimotor. Egocentrism = preoperational. Abstract morality = Kohlberg postconventional.
explanation.common_trap: Placing conservation in the wrong Piaget stage; it appears at concrete operational (~7), not preoperational.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A jury member initially unsure of a defendant's guilt shifts to a confident guilty vote after group deliberation. No new evidence was presented. Which social phenomenon best explains this shift?

choices.text: social loafing, in which individual effort decreases when working collectively
groupthink, in which the desire for group consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation
group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position
deindividuation, in which anonymity in groups leads to reduced self-awareness and more impulsive behavior

explanation.short: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk).
explanation.detailed: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Social loafing involves reduced individual effort in groups; this scenario is about opinion shift, not effort reduction
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Groupthink involves suppression of dissenting views to maintain cohesion; group polarization can occur even without pressure to conform, simply through discussion
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Deindividuation involves anonymity (e.g., crowds, online) reducing individual identity; this scenario is a deliberating jury, not an anonymous setting

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Group polarization: discussion → more extreme version of initial majority lean. Groupthink: pressure to conform → poor decisions.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing group polarization (direction determined by pre-existing lean) with groupthink (pressure-based conformity).
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: An observer sees a student fail an exam and concludes the student is lazy, not considering that the exam was unusually difficult. Which attribution error does this illustrate?

choices.text: the mere exposure effect, in which familiarity with the victim increases helping behavior
diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act
social facilitation, in which the presence of others improves an individual's performance on helping tasks
social comparison, in which individuals evaluate their prosocial behaviors against group norms

explanation.short: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies.
explanation.detailed: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The mere exposure effect increases positive feelings toward familiar stimuli; familiarity is not described in this scenario
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Social facilitation improves performance on well-learned tasks; it does not explain reduced helping in emergencies with multiple bystanders
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Social comparison involves evaluating one's own performance or opinions relative to others; diffusion of responsibility is the specific mechanism of bystander non-helping

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Bystander effect: more people → less helping. FAE: underestimate situation, overestimate disposition.
explanation.common_trap: Thinking larger groups are more likely to help; counterintuitively, more bystanders reduce individual intervention.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A student under chronic exam stress shows elevated cortisol, reduced lymphocyte proliferation, and increased rates of upper respiratory infections. Which pathway best connects stress to immune suppression?

choices.text: the sympathetic nervous system directly destroys lymphocytes through catecholamine toxicity
chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity
stress lowers insulin, reducing glucose uptake in lymphocytes and impairing antibody production
stress increases glucagon secretion, which diverts glucose from immune cells to muscle

explanation.short: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production.
explanation.detailed: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: While the SNS releases catecholamines during acute stress, lymphocyte destruction by catecholamines is not the primary mechanism; HPA-cortisol suppression is more significant in chronic stress
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Insulin affects glucose uptake broadly; the immune suppression in chronic stress is primarily mediated by cortisol's anti-inflammatory and lympholytic effects
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Glucagon raises blood glucose but does not selectively divert glucose away from immune cells; the HPA-cortisol axis is the primary neuroimmune link

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Chronic stress → cortisol (HPA axis) → immune suppression. GAS stages: alarm → resistance → exhaustion.
explanation.common_trap: Attributing all stress-immune effects to the sympathetic nervous system; the HPA-cortisol axis is the key chronic stress pathway.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A first-generation college student earns a medical degree and achieves income and prestige far exceeding their parents. Which type of social mobility does this represent?

choices.text: Weber identified class (economic), status (social prestige), and party/power (political influence) as three distinct, partially independent dimensions of stratification
Weber argued that religious beliefs (Protestant ethic) are the only meaningful dimension of social stratification
Weber proposed that biological differences between groups explain most variation in social position
Weber proposed that stratification is entirely determined by means of production, as described in Marxist class theory

explanation.short: Weber's tripartite model: (1) Class = economic position/market. (2) Status = social honor/prestige. (3) Party/Power = political influence. These can be aligned or misaligned (e.g., 'nouveau riche' has class but may lack status).
explanation.detailed: Weber's tripartite model: (1) Class = economic position/market. (2) Status = social honor/prestige. (3) Party/Power = political influence. These can be aligned or misaligned (e.g., 'nouveau riche' has class but may lack status). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: Weber identified class (economic), status (social prestige), and party/power (political influence) as three distinct, partially independent dimensions of stratification.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: While Weber analyzed the Protestant ethic and capitalism, he proposed the tripartite model of stratification as a distinct contribution, not religion alone
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Weber's stratification model is sociological, not biological; he emphasized social structures, not biological determinism
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Marx focused on means of production and class conflict; Weber agreed class matters but added status and power as separate dimensions

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Weber: class + status + power = three pillars of stratification. Marx: class conflict (bourgeoisie vs proletariat) = only pillar.
explanation.common_trap: Conflating Weber and Marx; Weber explicitly critiqued purely economic models of stratification.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: Research consistently shows that lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher rates of cardiovascular disease, even after controlling for behaviors like smoking and diet. Which explanatory framework best accounts for this residual association?

choices.text: structural and psychosocial mechanisms including chronic stress from financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and adverse neighborhood environments that persist independently of individual behaviors
lower SES individuals have genetic variants that directly cause cardiovascular disease
social mobility eliminates the health gradient because individuals can improve their SES over time
behavioral risk factors such as poor diet and smoking fully explain the SES-health gradient when properly measured

explanation.short: The SES-health gradient is robust and graded (each step up in SES improves health). Proposed mechanisms: chronic stress → cortisol → cardiovascular damage; limited healthcare access; environmental exposures; neighborhood quality; allostatic load.
explanation.detailed: The SES-health gradient is robust and graded (each step up in SES improves health). Proposed mechanisms: chronic stress → cortisol → cardiovascular damage; limited healthcare access; environmental exposures; neighborhood quality; allostatic load. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: structural and psychosocial mechanisms including chronic stress from financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and adverse neighborhood environments that persist independently of individual behaviors.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Genetics do not explain the graded, dose-response relationship between SES and health seen across the income spectrum; structural mechanisms are more consistent with the evidence
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Social mobility is possible but is neither uniform nor rapid; the structural mechanisms of poverty operate throughout the life course regardless of eventual mobility
wrong_answer_explanations.D: The residual association persists after controlling for behavioral risk factors; this is the key finding that points to structural causes beyond behavior

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: SES-health gradient: structural/psychosocial mechanisms persist after behavioral adjustment. Upstream = social structures, policies. Downstream = individual behaviors.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that controlling for smoking and diet eliminates the SES effect; a residual structural component remains.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: Howard Becker's labeling theory argues that deviance is not an inherent property of an act. What does it depend on instead?

choices.text: violation of a more, which carries severe moral condemnation by society
violation of a social norm enforced by informal negative sanctions (social exclusion), not a formal rule or law
violation of a folkway with a formal legal sanction
an example of secondary deviance, in which the labeled person internalizes a deviant identity

explanation.short: Norms: mores (strong moral significance), folkways (everyday courtesy, minor infractions), taboos (strongest prohibitions). Sanctions: formal (legal) vs informal (social approval/disapproval). Labeling theory: deviance is defined by societal reaction, not inherent to the act.
explanation.detailed: Norms: mores (strong moral significance), folkways (everyday courtesy, minor infractions), taboos (strongest prohibitions). Sanctions: formal (legal) vs informal (social approval/disapproval). Labeling theory: deviance is defined by societal reaction, not inherent to the act. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: violation of a social norm enforced by informal negative sanctions (social exclusion), not a formal rule or law.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Mores are norms with strong moral weight (e.g., prohibitions against theft, violence); interrupting conversation violates a minor social expectation, not a moral rule
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Folkways are informal norms; the sanction here (social exclusion) is also informal, not formal/legal; describing the sanction as formal is incorrect
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Secondary deviance (Lemert) refers to identity change following labeling; this scenario describes the initial social response to the behavior, not an identity internalization

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Folkways = minor norms, informal sanctions. Mores = moral norms, strong sanctions. Labeling theory: deviance defined by social reaction.
explanation.common_trap: Classifying all norm violations as mores; mores carry strong moral condemnation, while folkways are everyday courtesy rules.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A clinical trial recruits volunteers who respond to a newspaper ad. Compared to the general population, this sample skews toward healthier, more educated individuals. Which threat to validity does this represent?

choices.text: observer bias, in which the researcher's expectations influence data collection
selection bias (or sampling bias), which limits external validity by making the sample unrepresentative of the target population
social desirability bias, in which participants answer questions in ways they think are expected
attrition bias, in which differential dropout between groups distorts outcomes

explanation.short: Selection bias: the sample systematically differs from the target population, limiting external validity (generalizability). Random sampling reduces selection bias. Convenience samples (volunteers, clinic patients) are prone to it.
explanation.detailed: Selection bias: the sample systematically differs from the target population, limiting external validity (generalizability). Random sampling reduces selection bias. Convenience samples (volunteers, clinic patients) are prone to it. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: selection bias (or sampling bias), which limits external validity by making the sample unrepresentative of the target population.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Observer bias refers to systematic error in the researcher's measurement or interpretation, not in who is recruited
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Social desirability bias involves participants misreporting behavior to appear favorable; here the issue is who enters the study, not how they respond within it
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Attrition bias occurs when participants drop out differentially after enrollment; the issue here is who is enrolled to begin with

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Selection bias → non-representative sample → limits external validity. Hawthorne effect → behavior changes from being observed.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing selection bias (who enters the study) with attrition bias (who leaves the study); they threaten validity differently.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.

wrong_answer_explanations.D: Statistical significance thresholds do not determine whether causality can be inferred; study design (randomized vs observational) determines the causal inference capacity

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Correlation ≠ causation. RCTs can establish causation. Observational studies establish association only.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that statistical significance proves causation; p-values address whether an effect is real, not what caused it.

stem: A child who was bitten by a dog now fears all animals, including cats. Which classical conditioning process best explains this generalization?

choices.text: flooding, in which maximum exposure to the feared stimulus eliminates the response
stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus
higher-order conditioning, in which the conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus
spontaneous recovery, in which an extinguished response returns after a rest period

explanation.short: Stimulus generalization: CR spreads to stimuli resembling the CS (dog→all animals). Stimulus discrimination: learning to respond to CS but not similar stimuli. Both are normal parts of classical conditioning.
explanation.detailed: Stimulus generalization: CR spreads to stimuli resembling the CS (dog→all animals). Stimulus discrimination: learning to respond to CS but not similar stimuli. Both are normal parts of classical conditioning. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Flooding is a therapeutic technique involving prolonged exposure; stimulus generalization is a natural learning phenomenon
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Higher-order conditioning creates a new CS from an existing CS; generalization is the spread of response to similar stimuli without additional training
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Spontaneous recovery describes the return of an extinguished CR; generalization describes responding to new similar stimuli

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Generalization: respond to similar stimuli. Discrimination: distinguish CS from non-CS stimuli. Extinction: CS without US → CR decreases.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing generalization (occurs naturally) with overgeneralization in cognitive distortions; here it is a purely behavioral phenomenon.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A gambler at a slot machine responds at a high, steady rate that is highly resistant to extinction. Which reinforcement schedule best explains this behavior?

choices.text: fixed interval schedule, which produces a scallop pattern with bursts of responding near each reinforcement
variable interval schedule, which produces a steady, moderate response rate resistant to extinction
continuous reinforcement (fixed ratio 1), which produces rapid learning but the fastest extinction once reinforcement stops
variable ratio schedule, which produces high, steady response rates that are most resistant to extinction

explanation.short: Schedules: Continuous (FR1) → rapid learning, rapid extinction. Fixed ratio → pause after reward, then burst. Variable ratio (slot machine) → highest rate, most resistant to extinction. Fixed interval → scallop. Variable interval → steady, resistant.
explanation.detailed: Schedules: Continuous (FR1) → rapid learning, rapid extinction. Fixed ratio → pause after reward, then burst. Variable ratio (slot machine) → highest rate, most resistant to extinction. Fixed interval → scallop. Variable interval → steady, resistant. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: continuous reinforcement (fixed ratio 1), which produces rapid learning but the fastest extinction once reinforcement stops.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Fixed interval produces scallop patterns, not the steady, reliable responding of continuous reinforcement
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Variable interval produces steady moderate rates; continuous reinforcement is specifically every single response rewarded
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Variable ratio schedules do produce high, steady rates resistant to extinction, but this describes a slot machine; continuous reinforcement describes every-response reward

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: VR: highest rate, most extinction-resistant. FI: scallop. CR: fastest extinction. Fixed = predictable pause.
explanation.common_trap: Thinking continuous reinforcement is best for maintaining behavior long-term; it actually produces fastest extinction.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Memory Scenario
passage.text: A study examines memory using a randomized clinical study. Investigators are specifically interested in distinguishing undefined from related phenomena.

stem: A student studies for an exam in the same room where the exam will be held, performing better than classmates who studied elsewhere. Which memory principle explains this?

choices.text: proactive interference, in which old memories disrupt retrieval of new information
the spacing effect, in which distributed practice improves recall compared to massed practice
consolidation, in which memories are transferred from short-term to long-term storage during sleep
encoding specificity, in which retrieval is enhanced when the context at retrieval matches the context during encoding

explanation.short: Encoding specificity principle (Tulving): memory is best when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions (same room, same state, same cues). Context-dependent and state-dependent memory are related phenomena.
explanation.detailed: Encoding specificity principle (Tulving): memory is best when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions (same room, same state, same cues). Context-dependent and state-dependent memory are related phenomena. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: encoding specificity, in which retrieval is enhanced when the context at retrieval matches the context during encoding.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Proactive interference is when old memories block new learning; this scenario describes a context-match benefit, not interference
wrong_answer_explanations.B: The spacing effect describes better memory from distributed study sessions; the benefit here is context matching, not spacing
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Consolidation explains why sleep improves memory; the effect described is about environmental context at retrieval
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Encoding specificity: memory is cue-dependent. Motor skills = procedural (implicit, basal ganglia/cerebellum). Episodic memories = declarative (explicit, hippocampus).
explanation.common_trap: Confusing context-dependent memory with mnemonics; encoding specificity is about environmental/internal state matching.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: After learning a list of new vocabulary, a student forgets words from an earlier list learned the same day. Which interference type is responsible?

choices.text: proactive interference, in which older learned material (French) interferes with the encoding or retrieval of newer material (Spanish)
retroactive interference, in which newer material disrupts recall of older material
the serial position effect, in which primacy and recency determine recall regardless of similar material
motivated forgetting, in which anxiety about language learning suppresses both sets of memories

explanation.short: Proactive: PRO-old interferes with new. Retroactive: RETRO-new interferes with old (going backward). Memory tip: Pro-active = old moving Forward and blocking new; Retro-active = new going Backward and erasing old.
explanation.detailed: Proactive: PRO-old interferes with new. Retroactive: RETRO-new interferes with old (going backward). Memory tip: Pro-active = old moving Forward and blocking new; Retro-active = new going Backward and erasing old. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: proactive interference, in which older learned material (French) interferes with the encoding or retrieval of newer material (Spanish).

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts old memories; here old learning (French) disrupts new learning (Spanish), which is proactive
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The serial position effect describes recall patterns within a list based on position; it does not involve cross-list interference from similar content
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Motivated forgetting involves emotionally aversive material; learning two languages is not described as anxiety-inducing in this scenario

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Proactive: old→new disruption. Retroactive: new→old disruption.
explanation.common_trap: Reversing the direction; proactive interference comes from PRIOR learning, not new learning.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A radiologist improves at detecting subtle lung nodules on CT scans after training. Colleagues note the radiologist also develops more false positives. What does this change reflect in signal detection theory?

choices.text: improved sensitivity (d prime), meaning the radiologist is better at discriminating signals from noise without criterion change
the absolute threshold has decreased, so weaker signals now reach awareness
adaptation, in which repeated exposure to lung nodules raises the detection threshold
a lowered response criterion (liberal bias), meaning the radiologist is more willing to report a signal, increasing both hits and false alarms

explanation.short: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently.
explanation.detailed: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response criterion (β). A more liberal criterion → more hits AND more false alarms. A conservative criterion → fewer false alarms AND more misses. Training can shift either independently. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: a lowered response criterion (liberal bias), meaning the radiologist is more willing to report a signal, increasing both hits and false alarms.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Improved d prime would increase hits without proportionally increasing false alarms; the increase in false positives indicates a criterion shift, not sensitivity change
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Absolute threshold involves the minimum detectable stimulus intensity in isolation; signal detection theory addresses detection in noise, and criterion is distinct from threshold
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Adaptation reduces responsiveness to a repeated stimulus; training in detection improves, not impairs, task performance
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: SDT: d' = sensitivity (independent of willingness). Criterion = willingness to report. Liberal → more hits + more false alarms.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that 'better at detecting' always means higher sensitivity (d'); it may instead reflect a shifted criterion.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Structural basis for water permeability and ion exclusion in human aquaporin-1 determined by cryo-electron microscopy
passage.text: Structural basis for water permeability and ion exclusion in human aquaporin-1 determined by cryo-electron microscopy. Background: Aquaporin-1 (AQP1) facilitates osmotic water transport with high selectivity, excluding ions and protons by mechanisms not fully resolved. Methods: Human AQP1 in lipid nanodiscs was determined at 1.9 Å resolution by cryo-EM; molecular dynamics simulations modeled water permeation. Results: The selectivity filter pore narrows to 3 Å, lined by Asn76, Arg195, and His180. Water traverses in single file, reorienting midway to prevent proton conductance via the Grotthuss mechanism.

stem: The control condition in this experiment serves primarily to:

choices.text: the results cannot be generalized because the study used a non-human model system
the lack of a negative control means any observed effect could be due to handling alone
the correlational design proves a direct causal relationship between the variables measured
the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract

explanation.short: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation.
explanation.detailed: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Model systems have limitations but provide mechanistic evidence; failure to generalize is a concern, not an absolute disqualifier
wrong_answer_explanations.B: The study may have a negative control not explicitly mentioned; this extreme inference goes beyond the information given
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Even well-designed studies cannot prove causation from correlation; the word 'proves' is too strong and is a classic wrong-answer signal on the MCAT
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Evidence 'supports' a conclusion; it rarely 'proves' one. Always ask: what does the control group tell you?
explanation.common_trap: Selecting answers that use absolute language ('proves,' 'cannot,' 'always') when the data only support a probabilistic conclusion.

stem: A teenager argues that civil disobedience against an unjust law is morally justified based on abstract principles of justice. According to Kohlberg, which stage of moral reasoning does this represent?

choices.text: egocentrism, the inability to adopt another person's perspective
centration, the tendency to focus on only one perceptual dimension at a time
object permanence, understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight
conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance

explanation.short: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning.
explanation.detailed: Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0–2): object permanence. Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, centration, egocentrism, no conservation. Concrete operational (7–11): conservation, decentration, reversibility. Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: conservation, a concrete operational achievement (Piaget), understanding that quantity is invariant despite perceptual changes in appearance.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Egocentrism is characteristic of preoperational thought; conservation is the achievement that marks concrete operations
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Centration is the error the 4-year-old makes (focusing only on height); the 7-year-old has overcome centration, not exhibited it
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage (~8–12 months); the 7-year-old described is demonstrating concrete operational thought
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Conservation = concrete operational. Object permanence = sensorimotor. Egocentrism = preoperational. Abstract morality = Kohlberg postconventional.
explanation.common_trap: Placing conservation in the wrong Piaget stage; it appears at concrete operational (~7), not preoperational.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.text: A study examines social psychology using a randomized clinical study. Investigators are specifically interested in distinguishing undefined from related phenomena.

stem: A jury member initially unsure of a defendant's guilt shifts to a confident guilty vote after group deliberation. No new evidence was presented. Which social phenomenon best explains this shift?

choices.text: groupthink, in which the desire for group consensus suppresses dissent and critical evaluation
social loafing, in which individual effort decreases when working collectively
group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position
deindividuation, in which anonymity in groups leads to reduced self-awareness and more impulsive behavior

explanation.short: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk).
explanation.detailed: Group polarization: discussion strengthens pre-existing leanings. If most members lean guilty initially, deliberation shifts the group to stronger conviction. Different from groupthink (conformity pressure) and risky shift (specific form of polarization toward risk). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: group polarization, in which group discussion tends to strengthen members' initial leanings, shifting the group toward a more extreme position.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Groupthink involves suppression of dissenting views to maintain cohesion; group polarization can occur even without pressure to conform, simply through discussion
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Social loafing involves reduced individual effort in groups; this scenario is about opinion shift, not effort reduction
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Deindividuation involves anonymity (e.g., crowds, online) reducing individual identity; this scenario is a deliberating jury, not an anonymous setting

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Group polarization: discussion → more extreme version of initial majority lean. Groupthink: pressure to conform → poor decisions.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing group polarization (direction determined by pre-existing lean) with groupthink (pressure-based conformity).
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: An observer sees a student fail an exam and concludes the student is lazy, not considering that the exam was unusually difficult. Which attribution error does this illustrate?

choices.text: social comparison, in which individuals evaluate their prosocial behaviors against group norms
diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act
the mere exposure effect, in which familiarity with the victim increases helping behavior
social facilitation, in which the presence of others improves an individual's performance on helping tasks

explanation.short: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies.
explanation.detailed: Bystander effect: more observers → less individual helping. Mechanisms: (1) diffusion of responsibility (others will help), (2) pluralistic ignorance (others seem unconcerned, so maybe it's fine). Latané and Darley demonstrated this in staged emergencies. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: diffusion of responsibility in the bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each individual's felt obligation to act.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Social comparison involves evaluating one's own performance or opinions relative to others; diffusion of responsibility is the specific mechanism of bystander non-helping
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The mere exposure effect increases positive feelings toward familiar stimuli; familiarity is not described in this scenario
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Social facilitation improves performance on well-learned tasks; it does not explain reduced helping in emergencies with multiple bystanders

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Bystander effect: more people → less helping. FAE: underestimate situation, overestimate disposition.
explanation.common_trap: Thinking larger groups are more likely to help; counterintuitively, more bystanders reduce individual intervention.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A student under chronic exam stress shows elevated cortisol, reduced lymphocyte proliferation, and increased rates of upper respiratory infections. Which pathway best connects stress to immune suppression?

choices.text: stress increases glucagon secretion, which diverts glucose from immune cells to muscle
stress lowers insulin, reducing glucose uptake in lymphocytes and impairing antibody production
chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity
the sympathetic nervous system directly destroys lymphocytes through catecholamine toxicity

explanation.short: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production.
explanation.detailed: Chronic stress → sustained HPA activation → high cortisol → binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → inhibits NF-κB → ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, TNF) → impaired T cell proliferation and B cell antibody production. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: chronic HPA axis activation elevates cortisol, which inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppresses T and B lymphocyte proliferation, impairing adaptive immunity.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Glucagon raises blood glucose but does not selectively divert glucose away from immune cells; the HPA-cortisol axis is the primary neuroimmune link
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Insulin affects glucose uptake broadly; the immune suppression in chronic stress is primarily mediated by cortisol's anti-inflammatory and lympholytic effects
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: While the SNS releases catecholamines during acute stress, lymphocyte destruction by catecholamines is not the primary mechanism; HPA-cortisol suppression is more significant in chronic stress

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Chronic stress → cortisol (HPA axis) → immune suppression. GAS stages: alarm → resistance → exhaustion.
explanation.common_trap: Attributing all stress-immune effects to the sympathetic nervous system; the HPA-cortisol axis is the key chronic stress pathway.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A first-generation college student earns a medical degree and achieves income and prestige far exceeding their parents. Which type of social mobility does this represent?

choices.text: Weber proposed that biological differences between groups explain most variation in social position
Weber proposed that stratification is entirely determined by means of production, as described in Marxist class theory
Weber argued that religious beliefs (Protestant ethic) are the only meaningful dimension of social stratification
Weber identified class (economic), status (social prestige), and party/power (political influence) as three distinct, partially independent dimensions of stratification

explanation.short: Weber's tripartite model: (1) Class = economic position/market. (2) Status = social honor/prestige. (3) Party/Power = political influence. These can be aligned or misaligned (e.g., 'nouveau riche' has class but may lack status).
explanation.detailed: Weber's tripartite model: (1) Class = economic position/market. (2) Status = social honor/prestige. (3) Party/Power = political influence. These can be aligned or misaligned (e.g., 'nouveau riche' has class but may lack status). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: Weber identified class (economic), status (social prestige), and party/power (political influence) as three distinct, partially independent dimensions of stratification.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Weber's stratification model is sociological, not biological; he emphasized social structures, not biological determinism
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Marx focused on means of production and class conflict; Weber agreed class matters but added status and power as separate dimensions
wrong_answer_explanations.C: While Weber analyzed the Protestant ethic and capitalism, he proposed the tripartite model of stratification as a distinct contribution, not religion alone
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Weber: class + status + power = three pillars of stratification. Marx: class conflict (bourgeoisie vs proletariat) = only pillar.
explanation.common_trap: Conflating Weber and Marx; Weber explicitly critiqued purely economic models of stratification.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: Research consistently shows that lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher rates of cardiovascular disease, even after controlling for behaviors like smoking and diet. Which explanatory framework best accounts for this residual association?

choices.text: lower SES individuals have genetic variants that directly cause cardiovascular disease
behavioral risk factors such as poor diet and smoking fully explain the SES-health gradient when properly measured
social mobility eliminates the health gradient because individuals can improve their SES over time

structural and psychosocial mechanisms including chronic stress from financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and adverse neighborhood environments that persist independently of individual behaviors

explanation.short: The SES-health gradient is robust and graded (each step up in SES improves health). Proposed mechanisms: chronic stress → cortisol → cardiovascular damage; limited healthcare access; environmental exposures; neighborhood quality; allostatic load.
explanation.detailed: The SES-health gradient is robust and graded (each step up in SES improves health). Proposed mechanisms: chronic stress → cortisol → cardiovascular damage; limited healthcare access; environmental exposures; neighborhood quality; allostatic load. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: structural and psychosocial mechanisms including chronic stress from financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and adverse neighborhood environments that persist independently of individual behaviors.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Genetics do not explain the graded, dose-response relationship between SES and health seen across the income spectrum; structural mechanisms are more consistent with the evidence
wrong_answer_explanations.B: The residual association persists after controlling for behavioral risk factors; this is the key finding that points to structural causes beyond behavior
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Social mobility is possible but is neither uniform nor rapid; the structural mechanisms of poverty operate throughout the life course regardless of eventual mobility
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: SES-health gradient: structural/psychosocial mechanisms persist after behavioral adjustment. Upstream = social structures, policies. Downstream = individual behaviors.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that controlling for smoking and diet eliminates the SES effect; a residual structural component remains.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.text: A study examines norms and deviance using a computational pharmacokinetic model. Investigators are specifically interested in distinguishing undefined from related phenomena.

stem: Howard Becker's labeling theory argues that deviance is not an inherent property of an act. What does it depend on instead?

choices.text: violation of a social norm enforced by informal negative sanctions (social exclusion), not a formal rule or law
violation of a more, which carries severe moral condemnation by society
violation of a folkway with a formal legal sanction
an example of secondary deviance, in which the labeled person internalizes a deviant identity

explanation.short: Norms: mores (strong moral significance), folkways (everyday courtesy, minor infractions), taboos (strongest prohibitions). Sanctions: formal (legal) vs informal (social approval/disapproval). Labeling theory: deviance is defined by societal reaction, not inherent to the act.
explanation.detailed: Norms: mores (strong moral significance), folkways (everyday courtesy, minor infractions), taboos (strongest prohibitions). Sanctions: formal (legal) vs informal (social approval/disapproval). Labeling theory: deviance is defined by societal reaction, not inherent to the act. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: violation of a social norm enforced by informal negative sanctions (social exclusion), not a formal rule or law.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Mores are norms with strong moral weight (e.g., prohibitions against theft, violence); interrupting conversation violates a minor social expectation, not a moral rule
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Folkways are informal norms; the sanction here (social exclusion) is also informal, not formal/legal; describing the sanction as formal is incorrect
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Secondary deviance (Lemert) refers to identity change following labeling; this scenario describes the initial social response to the behavior, not an identity internalization

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Folkways = minor norms, informal sanctions. Mores = moral norms, strong sanctions. Labeling theory: deviance defined by social reaction.
explanation.common_trap: Classifying all norm violations as mores; mores carry strong moral condemnation, while folkways are everyday courtesy rules.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A clinical trial recruits volunteers who respond to a newspaper ad. Compared to the general population, this sample skews toward healthier, more educated individuals. Which threat to validity does this represent?

choices.text: social desirability bias, in which participants answer questions in ways they think are expected
attrition bias, in which differential dropout between groups distorts outcomes
observer bias, in which the researcher's expectations influence data collection
selection bias (or sampling bias), which limits external validity by making the sample unrepresentative of the target population

explanation.short: Selection bias: the sample systematically differs from the target population, limiting external validity (generalizability). Random sampling reduces selection bias. Convenience samples (volunteers, clinic patients) are prone to it.
explanation.detailed: Selection bias: the sample systematically differs from the target population, limiting external validity (generalizability). Random sampling reduces selection bias. stem: In a randomized controlled trial, an experimental drug reduces cholesterol by 30 mg/dL (p = 0.001, 95% CI: 20–40 mg/dL). Which statement best interprets these results?

choices.text: correlation does not imply causation; the association could be confounded by socioeconomic factors that independently predict both fast-food density and obesity rates
the sample size was too small to detect a true causal relationship
the study was not double-blinded, so placebo effects could explain the obesity rates
causal conclusions require p < 0.001, and this threshold was not specified in an observational study

explanation.short: Observational studies establish associations, not causation. Establishing causation requires ruling out confounders, reverse causation, and chance. The Bradford Hill criteria (strength, consistency, temporality, plausibility, etc.) guide causal inference.
explanation.detailed: Observational studies establish associations, not causation. Establishing causation requires ruling out confounders, reverse causation, and chance. The Bradford Hill criteria (strength, consistency, temporality, plausibility, etc.) guide causal inference. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: correlation does not imply causation; the association could be confounded by socioeconomic factors that independently predict both fast-food density and obesity rates.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Sample size affects statistical power but cannot make a correlation into causation; a large observational study still cannot establish causality
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Blinding is relevant in interventional studies; this is an observational correlation study where blinding does not apply
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Statistical significance thresholds do not determine whether causality can be inferred; study design (randomized vs observational) determines the causal inference capacity

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Correlation ≠ causation. RCTs can establish causation. Observational studies establish association only.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming that statistical significance proves causation; p-values address whether an effect is real, not what caused it.

stem: A child who was bitten by a dog now fears all animals, including cats. Which classical conditioning process best explains this generalization?

choices.text: stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus
higher-order conditioning, in which the conditioned stimulus is paired with a new neutral stimulus
spontaneous recovery, in which an extinguished response returns after a rest period
flooding, in which maximum exposure to the feared stimulus eliminates the response

explanation.short: Stimulus generalization: CR spreads to stimuli resembling the CS (dog→all animals). Stimulus discrimination: learning to respond to CS but not similar stimuli. Both are normal parts of classical conditioning.
explanation.detailed: Stimulus generalization: CR spreads to stimuli resembling the CS (dog→all animals). Stimulus discrimination: learning to respond to CS but not similar stimuli. Both are normal parts of classical conditioning. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: stimulus generalization, in which a conditioned response is elicited by stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Higher-order conditioning creates a new CS from an existing CS; generalization is the spread of response to similar stimuli without additional training
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Spontaneous recovery describes the return of an extinguished CR; generalization describes responding to new similar stimuli
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Flooding is a therapeutic technique involving prolonged exposure; stimulus generalization is a natural learning phenomenon

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Generalization: respond to similar stimuli. Discrimination: distinguish CS from non-CS stimuli. Extinction: CS without US → CR decreases.
explanation.common_trap: Confusing generalization (occurs naturally) with overgeneralization in cognitive distortions; here it is a purely behavioral phenomenon.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.
